top_choice_rationale: P003 (Autor, Dorn, Hanson) credits a well-bounded causal object: local labour-market evidence on how import competition and technological change affect employment, earnings, migration and adjustment. Over a decade of replication, extension and challenge supports its maturity. The citation is deliberately narrow, covering local effects and not aggregate welfare or the whole task and skill-premium lineage. The costs are real. Katz and the Acemoglu-Restrepo task lineage are left outside the credited set, and the size and persistence of the estimates are still debated. P001 (Helpman, Melitz) is a close second. It has the cleaner two-name credit set and a mechanism that has been tested directly on firm microdata, but Bernard, Eaton, Jensen and Kortum have serious claims on adjacent work, and the 2008 trade prize raises an overlap question. P002 is the largest influence on policy practice, but its attribution is diffuse and the micro evidence on its credited building blocks is mixed. P004 is cleanly attributed but its direct empirical identification is weaker. No award is ranked last because every proposal is a mature and substantive contribution.
recusal_note: No co-authorship or institutional tie to Autor, Dorn, Hanson, Katz, Helpman, Melitz, Woodford, Taylor, Calvo, Kiyotaki or Moore appears in my profile. My field of empirical labour economics is adjacent to P003, and as chair I gave the 2021 presentation speech on natural experiments, which may predispose me toward design-based evidence. I overlapped at Stockholm University (2010-17) with the IIES macro group (Hassler, Krusell), an institutional overlap and not a co-authorship. Not adjudicated.
